title: Coding agents are entering the delivery workflow; the gains still need checking
question: What has changed in coding-agent delivery, and what should a small team take from it?
argument: Recent accounts show coding agents being fitted into more of the delivery workflow: developers can shape project context and checks, use agents in browser tasks, and connect voice-driven work to visual previews and pull-request review. These examples make bounded experimentation more practical, but they do not establish general productivity gains. Teams should expand uses when their own measurements show quality is preserved and total effort falls.
synthesis: The sources describe different parts of a workflow shift rather than one proven productivity result. GitHub documents ways to supply repository rules, repeatable procedures, specialized agents, and browser tools. Simon Willison’s account shows voice and visual preview helping with an individual feature, while keyboard-based pull-request review still caught a design choice he changed. Asana reports a large cost and runtime reduction in a repeated browser task, and Flywire describes placing agents inside deterministic steps with restricted review permissions and human approval. Together, these accounts suggest teams can now experiment with agents across more workflow stages, while preserving review and measuring outcomes at each stage. The examples are implementation guidance, practitioner experience, and attributed vendor results—not evidence of a common delivery gain.
limitations: The evidence comes from vendor accounts, one practitioner’s project, and a machine-transcribed vendor video; it does not provide a controlled comparison of end-to-end delivery by small teams. Asana’s reported results concern a fixed catalog task and estimated model costs, not total delivery cost or general coding productivity. The Flywire transcript has not been audio-verified, so its claims should be read as attributed transcript evidence. These limits could change as independent, condition-matched small-team comparisons become available.

claims.statement: source_claim: GitHub’s tutorial presents repository and path-specific instructions, skills for repeatable procedures, specialized agents, and MCP connections such as Playwright as ways to tailor Copilot to a project; the supplied passages do not establish that these options are newly introduced or improve delivery outcomes.

That gives it a way to verify not only that the code passes automated checks, but also that the updated interface behaves as expected.

- Custom instructions define the conventions Copilot should follow across the repository or for particular files.
- Agent skills package repeatable procedures that Copilot can load when they’re relevant.
- Custom agents provide focused expertise and guidance for broader tasks.
- MCP servers connect Copilot to external tools, services, and data sources, expanding what Copilot can do.

MCP servers connect Copilot to external tools, data sources, and services. A documentation server can give it access to framework guidance, while a server such as Playwright can let it open and interact with your application in a browser.

claims.statement: reported_fact: In his account of one Django newsletter feature, Simon Willison says he used voice for about half an hour, then reviewed a pull request, changed an import approach, and spent another half hour prompting by keyboard before deployment. This is a single practitioner’s report, not a controlled productivity comparison.

locator.quote: We went on like this for about half an hour (the time it took to cook dinner).
It took an additional half hour of typing-based prompting to get to the point where I was happy to deploy it to production by landing the PR.

I reviewed the code in the GitHub PR interface. It was nearly what I needed, except it had chosen to use Git in a subprocess for one of the import scripts. I needed one of the imports to pull from a private Git repository, so I figured the API would be a better bet. I switched to typing and had Codex swap that out for an API-based import instead.

claims.statement: source_claim: Asana reports that its optimized GPT-6.1 Sol workflow averaged $0.47 in estimated model costs and about four minutes per run, compared with the original production setup on Model B, for a fixed task collecting six fields for each of 32 books. Those task-specific results do not establish a general coding-agent or small-team productivity gain.

locator.quote: The optimized workflow that emerged on GPT‑6.1 Sol averaged $0.47 in estimated model costs and about four minutes per run, 76x cheaper and 5x faster than the original production setup on Model B.
Each configuration performed the same task: collecting six fields for each of 32 books from a public demo catalog, representative of what some Asana customers run in StackAI.

claims.statement: source_claim: Flywire’s machine-transcribed video describes combining deterministic workflow steps with agents, and says people still review and approve merge requests. Its speakers also say a code-review step can read and search code but cannot edit files or push changes. These are implementation details from a vendor account, not independently verified outcome evidence.

inference: GitHub’s setup guidance, Willison’s account of moving between voice, preview, and keyboard review, and Flywire’s bounded workflow design together suggest that teams can try agents in specific delivery steps while retaining familiar review controls. Asana’s task-specific cost and runtime report shows a measurable dimension to track, but the sources do not demonstrate that these workflow changes reduce total effort while preserving quality; that is a question for a team’s own bounded trial.

locator.quote: Agent skills package repeatable procedures that Copilot can load when they’re relevant.
I still switch back to typing once I get down to the details of things though.

title: What the Numbers Actually Measure
question: Which recent coding-agent claims are supported by measured outcomes, and what remains unverified?
argument: The supplied evidence supports bounded claims about a fixed browser task, code-review evaluation methods, and GitHub-reported security trends. It does not establish general productivity gains for small teams. Teams can still experiment actively: measure quality and total effort on their own work, then expand uses when both support doing so.
synthesis: The Asana account reports repeat runs on one catalog task and records estimated model cost, runtime, and answer correctness; ReviewBench describes a versioned code-review benchmark and its validation approach. These measure different things, so neither alone demonstrates faster end-to-end software delivery. GitHub reports that credential-bearing pushes grew more slowly than screened pushes over its stated period, but that trend does not measure agent productivity. Separately, the Stack Overflow essay argues that a successful exit status can fail to verify an artifact, while Flywire’s machine-transcribed presentation says online evaluations were not yet in place. Together, these accounts support checking outputs and workflow outcomes, while leaving real-world gains to be established in the relevant team and task conditions.
limitations: The excerpts are sampled for several sources, so they cannot establish what those full sources do or do not report. Asana’s figures concern a single fixed catalog task and estimated model costs, not total delivery cost or varied small-team work. ReviewBench is a GitHub-authored benchmark; its described agreement measure does not independently establish production impact. GitHub’s trend figures are vendor-reported and the excerpt supplies no sample sizes or test details. The Stack Overflow piece is commentary, and the Flywire transcript is machine-generated and not audio-verified. These limits could be reduced by inspecting full methods and independently tracking task quality, review effort, rework, runtime, and costs in a bounded team trial.

claims.statement: Source claim: Asana says its 144-run study tested four models on the same task of collecting six fields for each of 32 books; the reported 76-fold cost and fivefold runtime comparisons use the optimized GPT-6.1 Sol workflow against the original production setup on Model B.

locator.quote: The optimized workflow that emerged on GPT‑6.1 Sol averaged $0.47 in estimated model costs and about four minutes per run, 76x cheaper and 5x faster than the original production setup on Model B.
Each configuration performed the same task: collecting six fields for each of 32 books from a public demo catalog

This is evidence about the reported secret-protection trend, not a measure of coding-agent productivity or proof of why the trend occurred.

claims.statement: Inference: The Asana and ReviewBench accounts describe different evaluation targets: a fixed browser task with reported cost, time, and correctness versus code-review benchmark construction and scoring. Because they assess different tasks and outcomes, their reported results cannot be combined into evidence of general small-team delivery gains; that conclusion would require measurements under matching team workflows and conditions.

Most benchmarks report precision and recall against a fixed golden set. ReviewBench reports six metrics in two families:

Before release, we asked senior engineers who had not participated in building the benchmark dataset to independently re-label every ground-truth finding from scratch. Their true/false-positive judgments agreed with ReviewBench 96.6% of the time.
We’re launching ReviewBench, a benchmark for code review agents built on representative GitHub pull requests, multi-source ground truth, calibrated evaluation, and production-aligned metrics.
Across experiments evaluated with ReviewBench before A/B testing, offline changes have consistently pointed in the same direction as what we see later in production.

claims.statement: Source claim and verification limit: The Flywire presentation transcript states that the company did not yet have online evaluations and describes them as a roadmap goal. This is a machine-transcribed media passage, not audio-verified evidence, and it describes Flywire’s account rather than a general industry condition.

title: A small trial should measure the work around the agent
question: What should a small team measure before expanding a coding agent’s role?
argument: Run a reversible trial on a recurring, bounded workflow, and expand only when observed quality holds and total team effort falls. Measure the delivered result, human review and rework, elapsed time, and full operating cost alongside safety and failure signals. This is an editorial recommendation, not a claim that supplied sources establish small-team productivity gains.
synthesis: The sources point to complementary parts of a useful trial. GitHub’s ReviewBench account describes comparing review systems with versioned evaluation components and metrics that reflect different precision-recall preferences; Stack Overflow’s field guide recommends baselines, CI evaluation, cost visibility, overrides, and a kill switch. Flywire describes deterministic workflow steps, read-only review access, and isolated component evaluation, while its speaker says online evaluations are not yet in place. Together, these accounts suggest a practical sequence: define a repeatable task and baseline, constrain what the agent can do, verify the artifact independently, then track quality, human effort, time, cost, and exceptions in actual use. The podcast adds deployment questions for a team considering longer-running agents: whether state persists across ephemeral runs, whether access to MCP tools is scoped, and whether sandbox boundaries contain failures. These are implementation observations, not validated small-team outcomes. Vendor examples from Asana and LegalOn show why cost and task conditions belong in the ledger, but their reported figures do not establish savings for another team.
limitations: This evidence does not establish that a bounded trial will improve productivity or that any proposed metric is sufficient by itself. ReviewBench and the implementation accounts come from interested publishers or practitioners; the podcast excerpts were sampled from a publisher-provided transcript and have not been checked against the audio. The supplied evidence offers no controlled small-team comparison of total effort, quality, and cost. Benchmarks and company-reported results describe their stated tasks and settings; they cannot stand in for varied team work. A trial should be stopped or narrowed if quality degrades, review or rework grows, access boundaries fail, or cost exceeds the team’s limit. Conversely, a longer or more expensive run may still be worthwhile if verified quality improves enough to justify it.

claims.statement: Proposed measurement: choose a recurring task with a clear acceptance check, record a baseline, and compare each trial configuration against it; retain the task, version, and evaluation setup so results can be repeated.

locator.quote: We version the benchmark dataset, judge, and matcher used in every evaluation, so results can be compared under the same benchmark configuration and revalidated when the benchmark changes.
You compare each release to a baseline, not just a pass/fail floor.

claims.statement: Proposed measurement: score the artifact against task-specific acceptance criteria and record human corrections, overrides, and rework as well as whether automated checks passed. A successful status alone does not show that the intended work was completed.

locator.quote: Don't let verification share a failure mode with the work.
You can see decisions, guardrail blocks, token cost, and override rate on a dashboard.

claims.statement: Proposed measurement: compare total human effort and elapsed time, including setup, waiting, review, fixes, and deployment, rather than treating model runtime or coding time as the whole delivery cost. The practitioner’s voice-driven feature account includes both an initial work period and additional keyboard review and changes; this is one experience, not a comparative result.

The report describes repeated configurations and recorded requests, traces, and results; these figures characterize that task and estimated model spend, not total delivery cost or a small team’s expected savings.

claims.statement: Proposed measurement: log model or tool cost per task and per delivered change, plus a hard spending limit and the behavior when it is reached. LegalOn reports task-based model routing, usage limits, and a feature-level customer-value metric still being built; Simon Willison describes hard caps as protection against runaway service charges. These accounts motivate tracking both cost and interruption risk, but do not validate a particular policy or cost saving.

locator.quote: The company is currently building the pipeline to calculate this metric.
These need to be hard limits.

claims.statement: Proposed measurement: test state recovery, tool permissions, isolation, time limits, and failure handling before allowing agents to run unattended or in parallel. The podcast guest describes external persistence for ephemeral agents, gateway-controlled MCP access, and sandboxed repository reviews; Flywire describes time limits, container limits, and read-only review access. These implementation accounts identify checks to try, not proof that either design is effective for a small team.
